newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian October labour force.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian October labour force.

text.p: Australian employment rose 25,500 in October and the unemployment rate was 8.8 percent, up from 8.7 in September, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Median forecasts had centred on a rise of 12,000 in employment rise and an unchanged unemployment rate of 8.7 percent. A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows:
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP SOCIETY:

"It definitely doesn't change the validity of the Reserve Bank's action yesterday. They were right to ease. The trend figure is still fairly soft and that's going to feed through into weak retail sales and on top of that you've still got unemployment still gradually drifting up towards 9.0 percent. I would think that there's a serious risk there of seeing 9.0 percent (unemployment) some time in the next six months."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"I think it's consistent with an underlying jobs growth of 10-15,000 but not much progress being made on the unemployment rate. This is the third month in a row that it has ticked up above 8.5 percent. The (RBA rate cut) decision was justified regardless of what happened today, but it basically underlines the fact that no real progress is being made in terms of unemployment at the moment. It affirms the need for a cut in rates and is one of the reasons that we still see a fairly good chance of another cut in rates early next year."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"We're seeing around about 10-12,000 in growth in employment per month which is just barely enough to keep the new entrants to the labour force and population growth in check, and therefore we see the unemployment rate stalled around this level, which politically is way too high. This will probably keep the speculation of another rate cut going."
PHIL GRAHAM, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ MCCAUGHAN:

"It could well be a bounce back from the bigger than expected fall last month. On the plus side the fact that it was split evenly between full-time and part-time jobs is encouraging. Looking at the interest rate outlook from here with yesterday's rate cut, we probably still need more information to be sure. Our feeling is that there is a good chance we will see another rate cut ... (but) not until February."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BAIN AND CO:

"I think the interesting thing is that you are still continuing to see full time employment growth coming back, or growing again. It probably bottomed in the March quarter. We would still expect a significant rise in employment next month as well. We went down (from a forecast rise in October employment) on the back of ANZ (job ads) and the retail trade numbers and so it came in a bit stronger than we were expecting to see. It just weakens off the growth we would be looking for next month. The fact that full-time employment is coming back up probably closes it (chance of near-term rate cut) off a little bit but you wouldn't be expecting any response even to the July rate cut in employment."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The jobs growth wasn't spectacular, especially given the fall the previous month and the unemployment rate continues to rise. It's just a sign that the economy is still firing on three out of four cylinders. What we need to see now is the rate cuts start to kick in and hopefully produce some confidence to create jobs. But we're not confident about that over the next few months."

"Despite the fact that the rise in employment was a little stronger than had been expected, it doesn't change the tone of our reading of the labour market and that is the labour market remains pretty soft. One signal is that of the 25,500 new jobs in October 21,000 of those were in female part-time employment. The other signal is that the underlying trend, excluding census workers, is only plus 7,000 jobs per month. If the economy is only creating 7,000 jobs per month that's roughly half of the rate required to achieve the government's employment forecast. It's not sufficient to get the unemployment rate down."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"Obviously, the major concern in these numbers is the unemployment rate has crept up again, but that's really because more workers have joined the workforce rather than any problem with employment growth. The unemployment problem will persist for time. We've probably seen the last monetary policy easing, but you can't rule it out yet."
